label.purpose: Uppercase meta rows, category counts, hours, captions, and credits.

narrative.overview:
Lyster looks like a menu printed on good paper and laid on a plain table: warm beige ground, one confident cobalt field, a brass rule holding the line. Familiar Swedish food is drawn once as a few flat ingredient planes with no outlines, so the plate can be read before it can be named. The page is bright and airy, never solemn; the luxury is in the craft, not in the lighting.

The system is deliberately undecorated. There are no shadows, gradients, rounded cards, or glass. Depth comes from flat tonal layers — paper against cobalt against brass — and from objects overlapping like printed sheets. Type carries most of the personality: one Swedish grotesk in monumental and whisper sizes, with a true italic for emphasis, tight negative tracking on the large end, and generous letterspacing on the small end. Layout is asymmetric and editorial, but always readable as a restaurant site first.

Motion is precise and editorial: the single plate draws its ring and settles once, section copy reveals as it enters, and the menu rail marks the current category. Nothing floats, bounces, or loops. If motion cannot clarify a change of state, it is left out.
keyCharacteristics: Warm beige paper ground with a subtle 128px noise texture.
Cobalt is a room you walk into (hero plate stage, proof band, booking band), not a global theme.
Brass appears as 1px rules, small dots, underlines, and one large disc.
Square corners everywhere; the only curves are circles (the plate, the photo crop, the discs, the mark).
One typeface, used from 0.68rem captions to a 12.5rem wordmark, with a real italic cut.
Exactly two authored glyphs: the brand Mark and one meatball Plate, used once.
Flat at rest: no box-shadows, no gradients, no glass, no rounded cards.

rules.name: The Paper Ground Rule
rules.body: Pages rest on Warm Paper. Cobalt is entered as a distinct band or stage; it never becomes the global page background.

rules.name: The Brass Line Rule
rules.body: Brass is a rule, a dot, an underline, a small inset panel, or one disc. It is not a body-copy color and not a page background.

rules.name: The Ingredient Only Rule
rules.body: Lingon, dill, and crust colors are confined to the food glyph and dietary tags. If a color could be eaten, it does not style chrome.

rules.name: The Two Registers Rule
rules.body: Type is either monumental (display and headline) or a printed whisper (label and supporting). Mid-sized decorative type is not part of the system.

rules.name: The No-Kicker Rule
rules.body: A heading stands alone. No uppercase eyebrow label sits above an h1 or h2 to explain it; the heading and the surrounding copy do that work.

rules.name: The One Object Rule
rules.body: Each composition has one dominant object — the plate, the photograph, a statement — and gives it real space. Do not fill the remaining columns with decoration, and do not repeat the object to create rhythm.

rules.name: The Clear The Header Rule
rules.body: Anything sticky or anchored must account for the 72px header plus the 64px menu nav; content never lands underneath them.

rules.name: The Flat Plane Rule
rules.body: No box-shadow, no blur, no glass, no gradient fills. If a surface needs separation, change its paper tone or put a 1px rule next to it.

rules.name: The Printed Overlap Rule
rules.body: Objects may overlap like misregistered print, but they stay flat. The plate sits on the disc; the photo sits inside the ring; neither casts anything.

rules.name: The Square Card Rule
rules.body: Cards are rectangles with no radius. If a shape needs to feel softer, use more space, not a corner radius.

rules.name: The No Side Tab Rule
rules.body: Never mark a card or note with a thick colored border on one side. Use a full-width hairline rule above it instead.

rules.name: The Italic Emphasis Rule
rules.body: Emphasis inside a heading is a true italic of the same family, usually in cobalt or pale brass. It is never a highlighter wash, fake oblique, or second typeface.

rules.name: The Two Glyphs Rule
rules.body: The site authors exactly two glyphs: the brand Mark and the meatball Plate. The Plate appears once, in the homepage hero. Arrows are typographic characters, the map is a live embed, and no other hand-drawn illustration is added.

dos: Do keep the page on Warm Paper (#f4eddf) with the 128px paper-noise texture; the ground should feel physical, not flat white.
Do use cobalt as a full-width band or a contained stage, and pair it with Chalk Paper text.
Do draw brass as a 1px rule, a dot, an underline, a small inset panel, or the single booking disc.
Do keep corners square and separation flat; change tone or add a hairline instead of a shadow.
Do use the circular plate and circular photo crop as the only curved containers.
Do set headings without eyebrow labels, and let the copy beneath them carry the explanation.
Do use the real italic cut for emphasis inside headings, in cobalt on paper or pale brass on cobalt.
Do keep the glyph count at two: the Mark and the single hero Plate. Let type, photography, rules, and the map do the rest.
Do give the mobile viewport the same hierarchy: one idea, one object, one primary action per screen.
donts: Don’t use a dark, moody food-photo hero or dim the paper ground to signal premium.
Don’t add box-shadow, blur, glass, gradient fills, or rounded cards.
Don’t use thick one-sided accent borders (side tabs) on notes, cards, or callouts.
Don’t let ingredient colors (lingon, dill, crust) escape the food glyph and dietary tags into buttons, fields, or section backgrounds.
Don’t fill large areas with brass; it loses its function as a rule.
Don’t add a kicker or uppercase eyebrow above a heading.
Don’t invent testimonials, awards, press logos, or a booking form that pretends to submit.
Don’t add another plate variant, decorative food glyph, or hand-drawn map.
Don’t remove the demo disclosure or the photo credit until real content replaces them.
